articles.headline: Iran developing chemical weapons, Israeli defense minister says
keyFacts: Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said Iran is developing chemical weapons and warned Israel may launch a preemptive strike to thwart the threat.
Iran's army commander said the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed to unauthorized traffic, while U.S. officials reported rising oil shipments.
Saudi Arabian authorities said 11 people were injured on Tuesday after Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- Saudi Arabian authorities said 11 people were injured Tuesday in a strike by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels that hit a tower in Riyadh's Financial District. Yemen's civil war has intensified since the summer, with the Iranian proxy group threatening to choke off oil and gas shipments from Saudi Arabia.

- Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Tuesday that Iran is developing chemical weapons, and vowed to stop Tehran from obtaining them. Iran has repeatedly denied they are developing chemical weapons.

- The commander of Iran's army reiterated on Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz is closed to all unauthorized traffic and will remain closed until Iran's seven conditions are met, and he appeared to call for Iranian forces to step up their attacks on commercial ships in the vital waterway.
Oil tanker traffic through Strait of Hormuz continues to rise, U.S. officials say
As Brent crude continues to hover around $90, its lowest level since late August, the U.S. continues to increase the amount of oil it is bringing out from the Persian Gulf.

Despite the number of attacks on tankers attempting to pass through the strait reaching their highest level in October — and with November already on pace to exceed that number — U.S. officials insist substantial oil is getting through.

"Last week was a notable one for tankers. More than 108 million barrels of crude oil were shipped through the strait by Gulf partners with U.S. protection, the largest weekly volume to date," U.S. Central Command spokesman Tim Hawkins said, referring to the date of the start of the conflict in February.

Since declaration of a ceasefire on April 7, more than 8,000 commercial vessels have transited the strait — about half under U.S. protection, according to a U.S. official. The official said more than 95% of ships are passing through the strait without any issue.
Iran developing chemical weapons, Israeli defense minister says, warns of possible preemptive strike
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Tuesday that Iran is developing chemical weapons, and vowed to stop Tehran from obtaining them.

"Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons," Katz said in a briefing to Israeli reporters, according to public broadcaster KAN and other national outlets. "The state of Israel will not allow them to reach that capability."
In his briefing on Tuesday, Katz floated the possibility of a preemptive strike against Tehran, if necessary.

"If we recognize that the Iranians intend to attack Israel, can't we tell the army to attack earlier and thwart the threat?" he said, according to a transcript from Israel's Channel 12. "If the Iranians attack us first, it will be a failure."

Katz's comments came at the same time as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi criticized the U.S. government for not funding the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, the international body that monitors and combats chemical weapons use at The Hague. The organization is facing a budget crisis because the U.S. has pulled funding, according to a Reuters report.

"The U.S. is so concerned about chemical arms that it's crippling the world's chemical weapons watchdog," Araghchi wrote Tuesday on X. "OPCW may be forced to suspend work and scale back vital programs. By obstructing its mandate, the U.S. is deliberately putting global peace and security at risk. Shameful."
The OPCW won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013 for its work in Syria.
CBS/AFP
Iranian singer lashed for "outraging public decency" becomes "a symbol of resistance"

Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed 74 times on Monday after being convicted of the crime of "outraging public decency" for performing without the head covering that is mandatory for women in the country.

Ahmadi was dealt the corporal punishment for her chosen attire during a livestreamed concert in 2024, according to her attorney, who was quoted by the reformist Iranian newspaper Emtemad on Monday. But Iranian women who spoke with CBS News on Tuesday said she was punished not for breaking the rule, but for daring to publicly defy the country's repressive regime — defiance that has made her "a symbol of resistance."

Ahmadi's lawyer told Emtemad that the singer and four members of her production team presented themselves to provincial authorities in the holy city of Qom, as required after their sentences were upheld in September by a local criminal court.
Iran army chief says Strait of Hormuz "must become increasingly closed day by day"

The commander of Iran's army reiterated the regime's stance on Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz is closed to all unauthorized traffic and will remain closed until are met, and he appeared to call for Iranian forces to step up their attacks on commercial ships in the vital waterway.

Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami said during an event attended by senior army commanders that Iran "did not allow the enemy to impose the pain of war solely on the Iranian people, but rather the warmongers have also felt the pain of war at their gas stations and in their living rooms."
In his remarks, carried by Iranian state television network IRIB, Hatami called on the Iranian Navy commander to make conditions in the waterway "more difficult."

"Until the Islamic Republic of Iran's seven conditions are met, not only will the Strait of Hormuz remain closed, but it must become increasingly closed day by day," he said. "Conditions must become more difficult for the enemy, and stronger control must be exercised over it."
11 injured in Houthi attack on Riyadh financial district tower, Saudi authorities say
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense agency said a strike by Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen on a building in Riyadh's Financial District left 11 people injured on Tuesday.
The injured included two Saudi citizens, two Indian nationals, three Nepalese nationals and four Egyptian nationals, according to the agency.

The Yemeni rebels did not immediately issue any statement about the attack, but late last week they issued a "warning to all investment companies, investors and capital to leave Saudi Arabia immediately and move to safe countries."
Iranian general says U.S. forces will "remain within range of Iran's armed forces" even if relocated

The Chief of the General Staff of Iran's armed forces said Tuesday that the Islamic Republic would continue targeting U.S. forces wherever they are, even if they are moved from damaged bases in the Middle East to "more distant areas."

Major General Ali Abdollahi, in remarks carried by Iranian state television network IRIB, claimed U.S. bases across the region had sustained "severe damage" due to Iranian attacks, "and a considerable number of them were rendered inoperable."

"Any relocation of US bases in the region will not change the Islamic Republic of Iran's resolve to confront threats," Abdollahi said Tuesday. "Wherever these bases are stationed, they will remain within range of Iran's armed forces if necessary."
Photos in September revealed for the first time the widespread damage and destruction caused by Iranian attacks to buildings and vehicles at multiple U.S. positions across the Middle East.
The Defense Department's inspector a fresh report in September on the war that revealed "equipment losses" worth up to $3.7 billion — including nearly 60 aircraft.
Saudis say tower in Riyadh financial district hit in "terrorist attack" after Houthi threat

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels confirmed an attack on a tower in the kingdom's financial district Tuesday, after witnesses reported the capital's tallest skyscraper being hit.

"One of the towers in the financial center was targeted in a cowardly terrorist attack. The relevant authorities are currently inspecting the attack site," coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said in a social media post.
The Houthis urged people to avoid Riyadh's financial district late last week days after Saudi authorities accused the rebels of damaging a different skyscraper in the district with a previous strike.

"We renew our warning to all investment companies, investors and capital to leave Saudi Arabia immediately and move to safe countries," Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree wrote in a Telegram post on Friday. "Saudi Arabia is not safe except for the holy areas in Mecca and Medina."
Global oil prices drop below $90, continuing slow decline despite ongoing attacks on ships in Gulf

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, was trading below $90 a barrel Tuesday morning, near its lowest point since late August. Global oil prices have been on a downward trend since late October after hitting a peak over the summer near $120 per barrel.

The drop comes despite ongoing attacks on tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz, both by Iran targeting vessels it accuses of violating its restrictions on the waterway, and by the U.S. military as it enforces its blockade of Iranian ports.

Iran's threat to commercial shipping in the Persian Gulf region — which it has wielded as a weapon since the U.S. and Israel launched their joint war on the country — severely restricted global oil supplies for much of the conflict.

Since major hostilities eased over the summer, oil prices have eased — likely as independent monitors say the flow of oil from Gulf producers has increased steadily. The International Energy Agency says crude exports from the Gulf have recovered to about 74% of pre-war levels, and the agency expects oil market surpluses within months.
The rebound in supplies appears to be offsetting market concerns over Iran's ongoing attacks and threats to ships, and President Trump's repeated threats to renew U.S. strikes against Iran.
Value of Iranian currency plunges on black market after new sanctions announced
Iran's currency plunged on the black market Tuesday after the U.S. Treasury announced new sanctions.

The Treasury announced sanctions Monday against more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, alleged front companies and individuals said to be part of the country's "shadow banking" network. It said the network was "overseen" by Iran's central bank.
By Tuesday afternoon, the U.S. dollar was trading at around 2.82 million rials, up about 5% from around 2.68 million the day before, according to websites monitoring black market rates.

"While Iran's shadow banking system moves the funds generated by Iran's international trade, the Iran Center for Exchange plays matchmaker and guides these funds to their ultimate destination inside Iran," OFAC said.
Houthis accuse Saudi forces of killing 30 thoroughbred horses with airstrike on stable
A news outlet run by Iran's Houthi rebel allies accused Saudi forces on Tuesday of killing 30 thoroughbred horses with a strike that hit a stable in Yemen.

Al-Masirah TV, which is owned by the Houthis, said Saudi aircraft conducted strikes in Sanaa and Amran that targeted civilian properties. Al-Masirah labelled the strike as a Saudi crime and said the horses held material and sentimental value.

The Houthis have been locked in grueling, more than decade-long civil war against Yemen's government forces, who are backed by Saudi Arabia. Recent Houthi gains have consolidated the group's control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which the group has tried to use to disrupt Saudi oil exports.
In a separate report, Al-Misarah said 1,421 civilians have been killed by Saudi strikes in Yemen since Sept. 2, citing the Houthi-controlled Yemeni Ministry of Health and Environment.
Rubio meets Qatari leader in Washington

Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with the Prime Minister of Qatar Monday in Washington - a regularly scheduled biannual meeting with a close Persian Gulf ally that comes as the tiny nation continues efforts to broker a deal between the U.S. and Iran.
Qatar, like most other U.S. Gulf allies, has faced attacks during the war by Iran, which has continued to threaten any country that supports American military operations.

The Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement Tuesday that Rubio had "reaffirmed the United States' commitment to Qatar's security," and underscored "the importance of the defense partnership in strengthening joint capabilities and protecting shared interests."

"On behalf of President Trump, Secretary Rubio expressed gratitude to His Highness the Amir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and the government of the State of Qatar for their leadership as a global mediator and close partner in advancing peace, stability, and security worldwide," the Qatari Foreign Ministry statement said.
Multiple ships reportedly struck near Strait of Hormuz

The British navy's maritime monitoring agency confirmed on Tuesday an attack on a tanker the previous day near the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran issued new claims of commercial vessels trying to use the vital waterway without its permission hitting sea mines.

The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center said a ship was anchored off the coast of the United Arab Emirates on Monday and that "a fire was reported onboard the vessel but no casualties have been reported at this time."
Meanwhile, the Iranian navy said two oil tankers caught fire after striking mines east of the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
The navy said the ship entered the strait "after disabling their identification and navigation systems."
Iran has previously struck ships in and near the Strait of Hormuz which it considers to be transiting without their permission.

The Iranian Navy said in a statement the waterway "will never be reopened until Iran's objectives and demands are met, and oil tanker owners are required to coordinate with the armed forces to ensure safe passage through this strategic strait."
U.S. reportedly investigating cyberattacks on oil tankers

The U.S. is investigating whether Iran is involved in cyberattacks targeting dozens of ships carrying oil and other explosive substances, according to sources familiar with the matter quoted by the Wall Street Journal.

As many as 50 ships carrying oil, chemical products and other explosive substances are believed to have been attacked, the Journal reported, citing the sources. In some cases, ships have also received bomb threats.
According to the sources, Iran is the primary suspect of the incidents, while Russia is also seen as a possible culprit.
The Journal had previously reported two of the cyberattacks targeted ships heading to Texas in September.
Houthi media says 25 killed or missing after Saudi strikes
Houthi-affiliated news agency Saba said Tuesday that a Saudi strike on buses and trucks had left 25 people dead or missing in Yemen's southwest.
The Iran-backed fighters, who control swathes of Yemen, are battling a Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen's internationally recognised government.

"The toll from the Saudi enemy planes' targeting of buses and trucks in Wadi Mabaq, Lahj Governorate, has risen to 25 martyrs or missing, and six wounded," reported the Houthi-run Saba news agency, adding that the continued presence of Saudi aircraft over the area was hindering rescue efforts.
On Monday, the Houthi's military spokesperson Yahya Saree had reported the attack — without providing casualty figures — and vowed it would not go "unanswered."
Separate strikes on Monday killed 17 people and destroyed several buildings in the neighbouring coast province of Hodeida, the Houthis' telecommunications ministry said.
CBS/AFP
3 oil tankers struck naval mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran's navy says
The Iranian navy said in a statement carried on state media that three oil tankers hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, resulting in "explosions and massive fires."
There were no immediate reports of casualties.

Iranian forces have been attacking shipping through the strait in a campaign aimed at hiking global energy prices to pressure the United States, which has imposed a crippling blockade on Iranian ports.
On Saturday, three other oil tankers were hit in what appeared to be the latest Iranian strikes on shipping through the strategic chokepoint.
CBS/AP
Top Iranian diplomat calls land blockade of Iran "impossible"

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called a land blockade of Iran "impossible" in comments shared Monday, according to Iranian state media. He also said pushing back against U.S. sanctions "is the duty of the entire country and its people," state media reported.
"The best way to counter this pressure is to make those imposing sanctions lose hope of achieving their goals, so they know this tool is ineffective and will remain so," Araghchi said.
Qatar's prime minister returns to Washington for Rubio meeting
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister, in Washington, D.C., on Monday.

It was the Qatari official's second visit to Washington in recent weeks, after meeting with President Trump earlier this month. At the time, Mr. Trump had said he didn't see a reason to escalate the Iran war after the midterm elections.
Qatar has been a key mediator in indirect talks between the U.S. and Iran to end the conflict, which have stalled.
U.S. issues dozens of new sanctions against Iran

The U.S. Treasury Department issued new sanctions against a group of Iranian nationals and entities, which it described as front companies and exchange houses, on Monday. A list of two dozen names posted to its website included nine Iranian individuals in addition to businesses based, mainly, in Tehran and Dubai.

The Treasury said in a news release that the sanctions came as part of "a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks," which, according to the agency, allow billions to circulate internationally and "provide the regime access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions."

"Iran's economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking," said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement. "Iran's shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime. Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake."
Coalition fighting Houthis carried out hundreds of strikes in last few hours, Yemen says

The military coalition fighting Houthi rebels in Yemen carried out 647 strikes in the last few hours, the Yemeni government said Monday. The attacks included drone, rocket, field artillery and airstrikes, a government spokesperson said in a social media statement.

According to the spokesperson, those strikes "targeted militia positions, gatherings, fortifications and movements" and resulted in the "neutralization" of 122 Houthi commanders and members. More than 50 vehicles and pieces of military equipment were destroyed or disabled, the statement said.

In a separate statement, also shared to social media, Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the Saudi Air Force had carried out 67 airstrikes and missile attacks in the last 24 hours, and that dozens of civilians were killed or wounded.

Saree said the strikes killed and wounded dozens of civilians in targeted areas of Yemen's capital, Sana'a, as well as the governorates of Lahj, Taiz, Hodeidah, Saada and Hajjah. But the Yemeni government blamed the Houthis for a missile attack Monday in Taiz, where, its spokesperson said, two civilians were killed and seven others were injured in the village of Kahlan.
Houthis say death toll from Saudi attack has risen to 17

Yemen's Houthi rebels said the death toll from a Saudi attack on the Red Sea port city of Hodeida rose to 17 Monday. The Iran-backed fighters, who control a massive portion of Yemen, including Hodeida, are battling a Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen's internationally recognized government.

Coalition airstrikes on telecommunication facilities killed 17 workers, wounded 11 more and caused the "total destruction" of administrative buildings, staff housing, a mosque and other infrastructure on the compound, the Houthis' telecommunications ministry said.
"This has led to the complete destruction of these facilities [and] the disruption of telecommunications and internet services," affecting tens of thousands of people, it said.

Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said in a social media post that another alleged Saudi coalition attack in the Lahj province, in Yemen's southwest, targeted buses and other vehicles. He said there were unspecified casualties.
Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment on either of the purported attacks. The coalition said Sunday that it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched at Saudi Arabia's western Red Sea coast.
CBS/AFP
U.S. discussing training Syrian armed forces, Reuters reports

The United States is discussing plans to train Syrian soldiers to conduct demining work, five people familiar with the matter told the Reuters news agency. The plan could see a small number of U.S. troops return to Syria as soon as next year if it is adopted.

The proposal is for a multinational training mission – made up of 15 countries including the U.K., France and Saudi Arabia – to focus on demining and ordnance disposal. It would be the first time since 2024 that U.S. troops had trained Syrian counterparts.
The U.S. State Department told Reuters that Washington welcomed having a partner in the Syrian capital, , who is committed to combating the terror group ISIS.
U.S. officials would need to do due diligence to screen all prospective Syrian recipients of the training before any funding is dedicated to the prospective project, two of the sources told Reuters.
Iranian singer convicted of "outraging public decency" lashed 74 times for performing without hijab

An Iranian singer has been lashed 74 times after being convicted of the crime of "outraging public decency" for performing without wearing the hijab head covering that is mandatory for women in the country.
Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed Monday over her 2024 live-streamed YouTube concert, according to her attorney, who was quoted by the reformist Iranian newspaper Etemad.

The lawyer told Etemad that Ahmadi and four members of her production team presented themselves to provincial authorities in the holy city of Qom Monday as required after their sentences were upheld in September by a local criminal court.
The criminal court in Qom upheld the convictions for "outraging public decency" citing "immoral" content posted online during Ahmadi's performance in December 2024, which went viral in Iran.
In addition to the 74 lashes, Parastoo and eight members of her team were also sentenced to a two-year ban on travel out of the country and a two-year ban on all "artistic activity."

Parastoo performed her concert in the Dayr-Gachin Caravanserai - an ancient site along the Silk Road route in Iran. It included themes of nationalism and popular uprising, and saw her openly flout both the Islamic Republic's dress code and a long-standing ban on women singing in public.
Netanyahu warns against downplaying "grave threats" facing Israel
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's now-caretaker prime minister, said Monday that Israel is still facing "serious and grave threats," and he warned of the dangers of downplaying them.

He spoke shortly after his domestic political opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, said he saw no immediate threat posed by Iran that would warrant military action before a new Israeli government is formed to oust Netanyahu.

"Anyone who belittles or downplays these immediate, serious and grave threats surrounding us does so for political reasons," Netanyahu said at a briefing in Israel's parliament, in which he called for a unity government, as Eisenkot attempts to form a new ruling coalition.
CBS/AFP
Netanyahu foe trying to form new Israeli government says no "immediate threat" requiring action against Iran

Gadi Eisenkot, the Israeli politician trying to form a new government to oust current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the wake of national elections, has said he sees no "immediate threat" from Iran requiring military action.
Speaking at a meeting of his party, Yashar, Monday, he said: "I see no direct and immediate threat from Iran today that would require Israel to act before a new government is formed."
He added that "the gravest threat Iran poses" comes from its stockpile of enriched uranium: "That is where we need to focus."
Netanyahu has appeared keen to go on the offensive against Iran again. Sources familiar with the matter told CBS News last week that Israel and the U.S. were .

Eisenkot recently said Netanyahu should not make any big national security decisions in the transition period following Israel's election, in which Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority, and that the now-caretaker prime minister should avoid "dangerous steps that can wait for the swearing in of a new government."
Iran seeks $290 billion in damages against the U.S.

Iran is due $290 billion from the United States to cover damages inflicted both during, and long before the war launched jointly by the U.S. and Israel almost nine months ago, Iran's judiciary authorities say.
Iranian courts have demanded the U.S. pay the sum, a judiciary official said Monday.

"We have secured court rulings in domestic courts awarding $290 billion in damages against the Americans," said Hassan Abdolianpour, head of the judiciary's center for lawyers, according to state television.
He also said several lawsuits had been filed against Persian Gulf Arab nations for "allowing their territory to be used by America to launch attacks against Iran."
According to state TV, the damages cover U.S. actions going back decades.

On Monday, state broadcaster IRIB said several U.S.-linked commercial ships had been seized and that part of the compensation owed to Iran would be settled through the seizures, without giving further details.
CBS/AFP
Lebanon denounces Israeli military official's visit to school in south
Lebanese officials have denounced a visit by an Israeli military spokesperson to a school in an Israeli-occupied area of southern Lebanon.

As Lebanon marked its independence day on Sunday, the Israeli military's Arabic-language spokesperson Ella Waweya shared a video on social media showing her outside a school in Debl, a Christian village, and then standing in front of a classroom full of children.

The village is located inside a wide swath of southern Lebanon that Israel has occupied and declared a "security zone" after the latest war erupted with Hezbollah in March. The zone covers a strip of southern Lebanon along the border and stretches about six miles into Lebanese territory.

Debl is among a number of Christian-majority villages near the border where many residents have refused to leave despite Israeli military orders to evacuate. Cut off from the rest of Lebanon, they are largely dependent on humanitarian aid.

"During my last visit to south Lebanon, I was amazed by the beauty of the land and the villages which have paid a heavy price due to their exploitation ... by a terrorist organization," Waweya said, referring to the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam denounced Israel for "dragging students into a military and propaganda display."
"An occupying power has no right to exploit our children to embellish the image of its occupation or impose its dominance over our people in the south," he added.

Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war in March with rocket fire at Israel, which responded with massive airstrikes and a ground invasion. Lebanon says Israeli attacks since then have killed more than 4,300 people.
CBS/AFP
Iran says it will use "all available means" to counter U.S. blockade
Iran said Monday it would use all means at its disposal to counter a U.S. naval blockade imposed in retaliation for its own push to block the Strait of Hormuz.
"We will certainly not tolerate these actions and will use all available means to counter U.S. aggression," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in his weekly press briefing.
Soon after the war broke out, the Strait of Hormuz became the focus of the conflict, with Iran continuing in its efforts to blockade the waterway, vital to global energy supplies.
In response, the U.S. imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports. It later announced a raft of economic sanctions, and launched a task force to disrupt land routes into Iran.

"You should bear in mind that what the Americans have described as economic sanctions, an economic blockade and a naval blockade undoubtedly constitutes an act of military aggression against Iran," said Baqaei. "Under these circumstances, Iran is entitled, pursuant to Article 51 of the U.N. Charter, to use any means at its disposal to defend itself."
Iran has said Hormuz could be open within two days but only if Washington agreed to its list of demands, which include the lifting of the blockade.
Houthi media say 4 dead in Saudi attack on key port city
Houthi media said Monday that a Saudi attack killed four people and wounded 18 in Yemen's key port city of Hodeida.
The Iran-backed fighters, who control large swathes of Yemen including Hodeida, are battling a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognized government.
The strike targeted a building belonging to Yemen's Public Telecommunications Corporation, the Houthis' Almasirah television channel wrote on X.
Riyadh didn't immediately comment on the report.
It came a day after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched toward the kingdom's western Red Sea coast.
That region is home to major oil installations that Houthi fighters have attacked in recent weeks, along with strikes on airports and military sites.
Yemen, which has been embroiled in more than a decade of civil war, was sucked into the U.S.-Iran conflict in July when a truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government unraveled.
Since then, hostilities have left more than 1,600 people dead and more than 300,000 displaced in the country, the poorest on the Arabian Peninsula, according to the latest U.N. data.
Houthis say Saudi strike on Yemen capital wounds 6
Houthi rebels in Yemen reported an airstrike early Sunday in the capital, Sanaa.
A spokesperson for the Houthi-run Health Ministry, Anees al-Asbahi, said the strike hit a fuel station operated by the state-run oil company and wounded six workers.
The strike also damaged the company's building, al-Asbahi said.
The Red Sea port city of Mokha also came under fire on Sunday, Houthi-run television reported, as did the Haifan district in the southwestern province of Taiza.
The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia for the airstrikes but didn't report any casualties from them.
Trump says Iran launched more drones and missiles in past week "than at any time for over a year"

President Trump on Sunday acknowledged that Iran "has launched more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time for over a year," but he added: "Don't worry, they've all been knocked down, and done no damage."
In a post on Truth Social, the president linked the midterm elections — in which in both chambers of Congress — to the escalation in the war with Iran.

"As everyone remembers, I predicted two things concerning the November 3rd Midterm Elections. One, that if the Democrats win, the Stock Markets would go down, substantially, which they have, and two, that the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has killed 81,000 protestors as of today, will grow more aggressive in their attacks, which has also occurred," Mr. Trump said.
Higher fuel prices triggered by the war caused economic concerns for Americans, and top Republicans, have partly attributed GOP election defeats to the war with Iran.
Mr. Trump on Sunday said voters "didn't understand" what their votes meant and called the election "very 'strange.'"

"Iranian leaders consider the Democrats weak, ineffective, and Country destroying, but I won't let that happen! Both the Dems and Iran fought like hell to keep the Oil price up as long as possible and, since the Election, the Oil price has dropped by a record level," he said. "Too bad the Voters didn't understand this before they pulled the trigger, but the whole Election was very 'strange.'"
Athlete swims Strait of Hormuz to raise awareness of Iran war's toll on wildlife

British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum in the North Pole and Antarctica to draw attention to environmental causes. But battling freezing waters and extreme conditions hasn't prepared him for his latest challenge: swimming the while tankers are attacked and blown up nearby.
Pugh, who is a United Nations Patron of the Oceans, spent three days this week swimming parts of the dangerous waterway to highlight how the threatens the area's habitat and wildlife.

Wearing only swimming trunks, goggles and a cap bearing the U.N. logo, the athlete started from the Musandam Peninsula, on the southern tip of the strait, and ended by rounding the Cape of Hormuz, completing about 9.3 miles in total. Pugh is believed to be the first person to undertake a long-distance swim there since the war started.
The swimmer said that minutes after he entered the water on Monday, he heard two loud explosions that rocked the sea.
Iran holds talks with Qatari mediators
Iranian deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Saturday that a Qatari delegation visited Tehran the previous evening and "held two hours of talks," without providing details.
Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran to end the war have stalled in recent months.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, however, that ongoing talks in the region must be "given a chance" and that the ongoing U.S. blockade of the Strait of Hormuz "must be lifted rationally."
"Our position is clear: as long as Iran's demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless," he said, quoted by state television.
"At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves."
Iran's conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the U.S. counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
CBS/AFP
Trump says he wants to make "permanent" deal with Iranian regime
President Trump said Saturday that he wants to make a "permanent" deal with Iran that will prevent the country from gaining a nuclear weapon in the future.

"What I'm doing is I'm going to make it so that if we have an incompetent president in four years or 15 years or 20 years, I'm going to make a deal that is going to be permanent," Mr. Trump told Fox News in a phone interview on Saturday. "I'm not going to let somebody allow them to have a nuclear weapon."

Mr. Trump said he's never "cared too much about the regime" leading Iran, and that he has "taken out two regimes already," though he declined to specify further. Former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the initial strikes on Iran that began the war in February 2026. His son Mojtaba Khamenei has held the title ever since.
Mr. Trump said Iranian officials have been "very, very difficult" to make a deal with.
"I mean, we make a deal and then they break the deal the next day," Mr. Trump said.

articles.headline: Who really owns the Albanian land Jared Kushner wants to turn into a 5-star resort?
keyFacts: Jared Kushner's partners bought 300 acres of Albanian oceanfront land for over $130 million to build a resort.
Albanian prosecutors and locals claim the land was illegally acquired through forged property titles.
An investigation by Albanian prosecutors into the forged titles could halt the resort project.
body: Who really owns the Albanian land Jared Kushner wants to turn into a 5-star resort?

ZVERNEC, Albania — In the summer of 2021, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump boarded a yacht owned by Nat Rothschild, an heir to the European banking family. On the way from Montenegro to Greece, the yacht anchored off the coast of Albania.
And, as Kushner told an investment conference last year, that's when Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama arrived at the boat to tell them about his plan for the country.

"I was very impressed by what he wanted to do with the country," said Kushner. "I really didn't know anything about the country and I didn't understand the history, and the darkness of the history with the communism and terrible leadership led to it being fully undeveloped as a nation."

A year later, Kushner was looking for development opportunities in the Balkans. He returned to the Albanian coast — to the city of Vlore, which was finishing the construction of an airport atop a wetland near an undeveloped coastline. "And obviously, a country's going to build an airport by the coast in a place they think is most beautiful," Kushner told the conference, "so we went there and we were looking for opportunities, and we found some incredible opportunities."

Kushner found those opportunities at Hidrovor Beach, an expanse of caramel-colored sand along the southern Albanian coast, with the gentle waves of the Adriatic lapping its perimeter and a view of an uninhabited island. A company working for Kushner purchased this land and 300 acres surrounding it for more than $130 million in April. But several people here tell NPR this is not Kushner's land.
They say it's theirs.
Land grabs and falsified documents

"This land here belonged to my family for centuries," says Gentian Mocka, who claims his family has owned this strip of beach and wetland since the time of the Ottoman Empire. He provided NPR land titles that appear to prove this.
After World War II, Albania's Communist government seized it — along with all private land.

When communism fell in 1991, families like Mocka's embarked on a years-long process to get their land back. "But then our problems started with the guys that were much more powerful than we were — had a lot of political support, were very rich and very well connected with the politics of that time," says Mocka.

In 2005, Mocka learned that someone else was laying claim to his family's land — a fellow Albanian named Artur Shehu. It was a familiar name for those who lived here in the 1990s, when the regional capital of Vlore was outside the control of the country's government. It was instead run by mafia-style gangs. At the time, Shehu was well-known to police in Vlore for his alleged involvement in a crime syndicate that, according to Albanian prosecutors, smuggled drugs and migrants into Europe. He fled Albania in 1999, after what police say was a shootout with a rival gang.

He ended up in the United States, where he received asylum in 2001 and, later, became a U.S. citizen. The 60-year-old Shehu now lives in a villa in Miami Beach. But he's continued to manage a growing real estate portfolio back in Albania through an associate in Vlore named Pellumb Petritaj.

The pair has claimed plots of land — including Mocka's family plot — up and down the southern Albanian coast, and prosecutors have taken notice. In 2018, Petritaj served three years in prison for forging land titles on behalf of Shehu. And on Nov. 18, Petritaj was sentenced to another seven years in prison for falsifying documents to $17 million worth of oceanfront property in the city of Vlore on behalf of Shehu. The court ordered the land — which does not include Mocka's family plot — confiscated from Shehu last week. The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.
Albanian prosecutors say land linked to Kushner may have been "illegally acquired"
The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.

The quiet village has only a couple hundred residents. Most of them, like Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota, are past the age of 70. On a recent warm and sunny afternoon, the two are resting on benches in the courtyard of the village church after a day of harvesting olives. They nod their heads when asked about Artur Shehu.
"He is from the village of Kanina, far from here and up in the mountains," says Konomi, motioning inland, "but his family has never lived here. He's involved in shady dealings."
Then Kota speaks up. "There wasn't a single soul of that family living here, going back to the Ottoman times," she says. "But we've heard stories about him, and we're very scared of him."

Twenty years ago, Kota, Konomi and dozens of others in this village learned that Artur Shehu had somehow acquired their farmland. They filed suit in Albanian court to reclaim their land, a fight that escalated this past April when Shehu sold the 300-acre parcel that includes what they say is their farmland to a company developing a luxury resort project for Kushner.
That transaction, however, is under review.
In court documents obtained by NPR, Albanian prosecutors argue that the land involved in Kushner's development is "suspected of having been illegally acquired through forgery."

A spokesman for Kushner did not respond to NPR's request for comment by the time this article was published. Kushner had previously issued a statement on his website saying his partnership purchased the land from a private party in a private transaction. "Title was reviewed by counsel and verified," the statement says.
Shehu did not respond to NPR's request for comment. He has previously denied any wrongdoing. However, in Tirana, a former lawyer for Shehu was willing to talk.
Oceanfront properties are now claimed by several parties

"The people that Artur [Shehu] has authorized by power of attorney to deal with his family's properties committed a forgery in which they removed the property from the brother of Artur's grandfather and passed it to Artur's grandfather," says Kujtim Cakrani. "That is the whole story of the property."

Cakrani says Shehu's associates forged an inheritance certificate that made it appear that Shehu's grandfather had owned the land, which was then passed to Artur Shehu himself. And then last April, Shehu sold that land to Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat, Syrian-born Qatari billionaire brothers who are financial partners of Jared Kushner.

Cakrani says that when he discovered that Artur Shehu was involved in this alleged forgery, he dropped him as his client. "I could no longer continue representing him because of the seriousness of the matter," he says. "It is impossible for me, with these documents that he has, to defend him."

And this is why, Cakrani says, Albanian state prosecutors have put Shehu under investigation and froze his bank accounts. Cakrani says he is now representing a group of 30 relatives of Shehu who he claims to be the rightful owners of this land.

Gentian Mocka, as well as Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota in Zvernec, tell NPR that nobody by the name of Shehu — neither Artur nor his relatives — has any legal claim to what they say is their land, oceanfront property that has now been claimed by several parties, including the son-in-law of the president of the United States.
Wealthy speculators have exploited land in Albania since the fall of communism
Albanian real estate law expert Roden Hoxha says he has seen this kind of land battle many times before. "But now that Kushner is in it," he says, "everybody is freaking out."

He says land ownership in Albania is complicated by decades under a Stalinist regime that stole all the land from private owners and collectivized it. When communism fell in 1991, he says Albania became a land grab free-for-all.
"It was basically chaos," he says. "People started claiming land wherever they threw a stone. It was basically the Albanian version of the U.S.' claiming of the West."

Hoxha describes wealthy speculators keen to exploit the chaos of the moment: locals whose families have farmed the land for generations and well-connected operators like Shehu, who aggressively try to claim that land. "And then on the international level," says Hoxha, most recently, "it exploded because it was Kushner and Trump and Arab money behind it."

And so, Hoxha says, what at first appeared to be yet another Albanian land dispute now has ties all the way to the White House. In the end, an Albanian court will likely decide who the rightful owner of this property is. But for now, it has sparked unprecedented public outrage in Albania. Protesters have taken to the streets of the capital, Tirana, every day since May 31, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. But Rama has only vowed to crack down harder on what have become increasingly violent demonstrations against his entire government.
Rama has also vowed that Kushner's resort project will go ahead as planned, but an ongoing investigation by Albania's state prosecutor into forged land titles could halt the project.

When contacted by NPR, Elona Sinaj, Rama's spokesperson, sent a statement saying, "If the seller does not have legitimate ownership of the property, the money will remain within the Republic of Albania, and certainly it will be used for anyone who proves that his claim over the property is grounded."
Sinaj went on to say that the ambition for Rama's government is "to create a new benchmark for sustainable Mediterranean development."
Some Albanians see advantages to having a Kushner-linked resort

That goal aligns with Kushner's vision for a luxury resort — a five-star ecotourism site, as his wife, Ivanka Trump, laid out in a podcast episode called "Ivanka Trump on Building the Authentic Life."

"For me," said Trump, "this is, it feels more like a challenge than anything else, the culmination of all of my experience in real estate, all of my travel, a lot of reflection on how I want to live."
In the podcast, Trump described both the Zvernec beachfront property as well as Sazan — an uninhabited island across from it — as part of a development project belonging to her and Kushner.

Local tour operator Sherif Durmishaj has made a living taking tourists to Sazan by boat, guiding hikes past foxholes and signs along the trail that warn of active land mines scattered throughout the island's forests. For years, this island was a fortified military outpost.
Durmishaj says he's seen the ongoing protests against the Kushner project, but he takes a different view of it.

"I work in tourism, and I'm from here," he says, "and if you've seen how local developers, along with the mafia, have built this region, it's just a massacre. They've destroyed so much of what is a beautiful coastline, and I support the Kushner project because it's going to be ecologically sustainable and it will set a good benchmark for future projects."
"We are a small country," Durmishaj says, "and Kushner and Trump are very big names."
At least one big name will be in the crosshairs of the incoming Democratic Congress in the U.S.

Regarding Kushner, "This is an individual in the Trump family who has essentially been two-timing on the American people," says Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is expected to chair the House Judiciary Committee and will have the power to investigate and subpoena members of President Trump's family.
He says he'll be focusing on Kushner, who he says has been splitting his time between foreign policy and making business deals on the side.

"American foreign policy has never seen anything like that before," says Raskin. "And in this, of course, he is only imitating his father-in-law, who declared that he got $2.2 billion on the side in his first year in office. Uh, that's more than $1 million an hour."

Raskin says the luxury resort project in Albania is one of many Kushner-backed deals that have prompted investigative inquiries from his committee, and there could be more as the new U.S. Congress is sworn in in January.
Fjori Sinoruka contributed to this report.

articles.headline: The First Squabble Of The 2028 Democratic Primary Is Here, And It’s Over 'Dark Money'
keyFacts: The Democratic National Committee introduced new guidelines requiring primary candidates to denounce undisclosed dark money spending to participate in debates.
Progressive lawmakers and party figures praised the rule as an important step, while some moderates criticized it as impractical and harmful.
DNC chair Ken Martin stated the policy will not end super PACs or dark money but aims to change the tone of campaign ads.
body: The Democratic Party’s attempt to quash the influence of outside “dark money” groups in the party’s presidential primaries split party strategists on Monday, with progressives praising new guidelines from the Democratic National Committee and some moderates questioning them.

The provision, which requires candidates to denounce such spending from super PACs or nonprofit groups that don’t disclose their donors on their behalf if they want to even be eligible to appear in the dozen planned debates, rolled out with plenty of institutional support, and Ken Martin, the DNC’s chair, have long called to excise non-disclosed cash from the party.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who failed to get her party’s nomination in 2020, called the requirement a “powerfully important step in getting Big Money out of politics.” Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) said the DNC was taking “a first step to make sure our Party answers to the voters, not billionaires and special interests.” Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.) called the move “long overdue.” Kendall Scudder, the chairman of the Texas Democrats who just oversaw several historic victories in the Lone Star state, lauded the decision.

The individuals who would be most impacted ― the potential candidates themselves ― were virtually mute on the issue. No major potential contender issued a statement or immediate reaction, though some of their allies weighed in.

Ammar Moussa, a senior press secretary for Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, scolded the decision, writing on X: “I love when Dems virtue signal so hard to the point they want to cost us elections.” (Moore is seen as likely to run but has said he is “still sorting it out.”)

Moussa’s comments were part of a wave of moderate skepticism about the rules, variously arguing raising outside money was an inescapable part of modern campaigns, questioning how the DNC could enforce the rules, fretting they would leave candidates vulnerable to potential attacks from GOP outside groups and fearing it would make candidates look hypocritical.

“This isn’t going to stop dark money in politics, it’s only going to force some candidates to talk out of both sides of their mouth,” said one party strategist who previously worked at the DNC, requesting anonymity to speak frankly. “When eventual front-runners are receiving outside support, it will also empower tier two candidates to attack front-runners on this issue when we all know outside money is going to be necessary to win a general election.”
The strategist said the plan made them worry about how Martin and the DNC would run the nominating process.

“The DNC should be focused on helping us find the strongest candidate who has the ability to leverage every tool in the tool box to win,” the strategist said. “Instead, it appears that they’re asking Elizabeth Warren’s permission to have debates. We’re off to a bad start.”
Other strategists worried it would handicap candidates who can not self-fund their campaigns ― in other words, almost every major potential candidate except Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker.
In an interview with MS NOW, Martin called the decision an imperfect solution, but one that aligns with the party’s values.

“Let me be very clear. It’s not going to end super PACs. We don’t have the power to do it. It’s not going to end dark money spending. We don’t have the power to do it. But it is going to require our candidates actually to also stand up and to say, ‘Look, I disavow this, and if it’s being spent in my name, I disavow it. If it’s being spent to attack my fellow colleagues who are running for this office, I disavow that,’” Martin said. “And that hopefully will change the tenor and tone of those ads and the conversations that are happening.”

And that view seems to have the support of DNC members: Former Biden White House adviser John McCarthy, himself a DNC member, wrote on X that the ban was a “small but meaningful step. And it’s a step in the right direction” and “an opportunity to enter that fight with a stronger nominee and a clearer set of values.”
